title: Sandboxes, Computers, and Terminals for Enterprise Agents
summary: Why enterprise agents need sandboxes, computers, and terminals for real work, with human review and deploy-anywhere controls for regulated teams.
body_markdown:
Most "enterprise agent" demos stop at a clean chat answer. Real queues do not. Operators need agents that can open a packet, run a validation script, inspect an export, call a narrow tool, draft a write-back, and stop for a human before anything hits a system of record.


**Take:** Chat-only agents that cannot open a sandbox or terminal will stall on real enterprise work. If the product cannot give an agent a computer-shaped place to work under policy, you are buying a conversational UI on top of retrieval, not an agentic workflow platform.


StackAI treats sandboxes, computers, and terminals as first-class parts of agentic workflows for regulated buyers: defense, banks, healthcare. Pair that with a low-code builder,[300+ integrations](http://127.0.0.1:8000/integrations) ,[MCP servers](http://127.0.0.1:8000/platform/mcp) , human review, and deploy-anywhere (StackAI cloud, VPC/private cloud, or on-prem with a HIPAA- and GDPR-ready posture). Primer:[what is an AI agent](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) .


## What sandboxes, computers, and terminals are for


**Sandboxes** are isolated places to build and prove a workflow on non-production data. Builders attach draft tools, break things, and iterate without touching core banking, EHR-adjacent systems, or mission stores.


**Computers** give agents a persistent workspace for multi-step work: files, browsers under policy, longer-running tasks that do not fit in a single prompt.


**Terminals** matter when a step needs scripts, CLI tools, or runbook-style checks that your operators already trust. The point is not "let the model sudo production." The point is controlled execution with logs.


Together they support atomized multi-agent org processes: one agent parses, another validates, another drafts, a human reviews, a narrow write tool commits. That is the opposite of a personal always-on agent that holds every app in one persona ([personal vs enterprise agents](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/personal-ai-agents-vs-enterprise-agentic-workflows) ).


## Why regulated buyers should insist on this


Banks fail when an agent "summarizes" a KYC packet but cannot run the structured checks your ops team already uses. Hospitals fail when a model drafts a note with no place to assemble documents under PHI controls. Defense programs fail when a demo cannot run inside an approved boundary with inspectable execution.

Least privilege still wins: domain-scoped servers, no shared production credentials in sandboxes.


## Design pattern we recommend


1.


**Build in a sandbox** with synthetic or redacted data.


2.


**Attach read and draft tools only** via integrations and MCP.


3.


**Use computers/terminals** for parsing, validation, and evidence assembly.


4.


**Add human review** before any system-of-record write.


5.


**Promote** workflow versions and tool pins together.


6.


**Place** the runtime where residency demands ([HIPAA/GDPR ready agents](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/hipaa-gdpr-ready-ai-agents) ,[deployment options](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/deployment-options-on-stackai) ,[/security](http://127.0.0.1:8000/security) ).


Governance is the control plane around all of this: SSO/RBAC, publish controls, audit trails ([governing AI agents at scale](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/governing-ai-agents-at-scale-how-stackai-keeps-enterprises-in-control) ).


## FDEs make the execution layer shippable


Giving an agent a terminal without delivery ownership is how you get a clever intern with root fantasies. StackAI[forward-deployed engineers and AI strategists](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/forward-deployed-engineers-agentic-ai) sit with operators and security to decide which steps need computers, which stay pure API calls, and which must stop for a person. They stay through the first production cohort when permissions break and reviewers push back.

## Failure cases you should run on day one


Do not celebrate a happy-path packet. Run these:


-


Missing required attachments


-


Conflicting field values across two sources


-


Downstream system unavailable


-


Permission denied on a write tool


-


Reviewer rejects the draft twice


-


Builder tries to attach a production write server in sandbox


A chat-only agent will bluff or stall. A StackAI-shaped workflow should stop, escalate, or show the failure in the review UI. That is what security wants to see before go-live.


Tie those tests to promotion rules: nothing moves to production without pinned MCP servers and workflow versions ([MCP servers](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/mcp-servers-regulated-enterprise) ). Keep insurance and legal packet examples in mind when you design evidence screens ([insurance](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/ai-agents-for-insurance-and-underwriting) ,[legal](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/ai-agents-for-legal-and-compliance) ). Defense buyers should run the same tests inside the candidate boundary ([defense](http://127.0.0.1:8000/blog/ai-agents-for-defense-and-gov) ).


## What to bring to a demo


Bring one workflow that is more than Q&A:


-


A sample packet or export (redacted)


-


The validation steps operators run today


-


The write-backs that require a human


-


Where the runtime must live


Book a[StackAI demo](http://127.0.0.1:8000/solutions/demo) . We will show sandboxes, computers, and terminals inside an atomized agentic workflow, with MCP scope and review gates your security team can attack early.


Chat is a surface. Sandboxes, computers, and terminals are how enterprise agents do the work chat pretends to finish.
